title: Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding
tagline: From subatomic particles and isotopes to the octet rule, electrovalent and covalent bonding, and orbit structures.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Chemistry syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Everything about how a substance behaves follows from how its atoms are held together. This chapter builds from the inside of the atom — protons, neutrons and electrons, mass number and isotopes — to the way electrons arrange themselves in shells, and then to bonding itself: the transfer of electrons that gives electrovalent bonding and the sharing of electrons that gives covalent bonding. You will learn to write electronic configurations, draw orbit (dot-and-cross) structures, and predict properties from the type of bond present.

facts.label: Subatomic particles
facts.value: Proton (+1, mass 1), neutron (0, mass 1), electron (-1, mass 1/1837)

facts.label: Stable configuration
facts.value: Outer shell with 8 electrons (octet), or 2 for the first shell

facts.label: Bond types
facts.value: Electrovalent (transfer of electrons), covalent (sharing of electrons)

blocks.text: An atom has a small dense nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons. Protons carry unit positive charge and have mass 1 unit; neutrons are uncharged with mass 1 unit; electrons carry unit negative charge but are so light (1/1837 of a unit) that they contribute negligible mass. Atomic number Z counts protons and identifies the element; mass number A counts protons plus neutrons. Electrons in a neutral atom equal protons, so Z also gives the electron count. Electrons occupy shells nearest the nucleus first: the K shell holds up to 2, the L shell up to 8, the M shell up to 8 for the elements in this course.

items.meaning: Number of protons in the nucleus; defines the element.
Total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
Atoms of the same element with the same Z but different numbers of neutrons, so different mass numbers.
An atom or group of atoms carrying a net charge because it has gained or lost electrons.
The arrangement of electrons in shells, written as 2, 8, 8 and so on.

items: Number of neutrons = A minus Z; number of electrons in a neutral atom = Z.
Isotopes have identical chemical properties because they have identical electronic configurations; they differ in nuclear properties.
Common isotopes: hydrogen-1 (protium), hydrogen-2 (deuterium), hydrogen-3 (tritium); carbon-12 and carbon-14; chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.
Cations form by losing electrons (Na to Na+); anions form by gaining electrons (Cl to Cl-).

items.text: Sodium: Z = 11, A = 23, so neutrons = 23 - 11 = 12; configuration 2, 8, 1.
items.note: One electron in the outer shell means sodium loses it readily, forming Na+ with a stable 2, 8 arrangement.

items.text: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 both have Z = 17 but 18 and 20 neutrons.
items.note: Average atomic mass of chlorine is 35.5 because chlorine-35 is about 75 per cent abundant and chlorine-37 about 25 per cent.

learn.title: Electronic configuration and the octet rule

blocks.text: Chemical behaviour is governed by the outermost shell. Atoms react to reach a full outer shell — eight electrons, or two for elements whose outer shell is the K shell — because that arrangement is energetically stable. Sodium (2, 8, 1) sheds one electron, magnesium (2, 8, 2) two, aluminium (2, 8, 3) three; chlorine (2, 8, 7) needs one, oxygen (2, 6) needs two and nitrogen (2, 5) needs three. The tendency to complete the octet explains why ions form, why elements in the same group behave alike, and why atoms combine at all.

items: Write configurations shell by shell, filling K first with 2, then L with 8, then M.
Elements with 1, 2 or 3 outer electrons tend to lose them, forming positive ions.
Elements with 5, 6 or 7 outer electrons tend to gain electrons, forming negative ions.
Metals lose electrons; non-metals gain — the two tendencies meet in ionic bonding.
Noble gases (2, 8) already have full outer shells, so they rarely react.

items.text: Calcium, Z = 20: configuration 2, 8, 8, 2; it loses 2 electrons to form Ca2+ with configuration 2, 8, 8.
items.note: Even though the M shell could hold more, calcium achieves a stable octet by emptying its outermost shell.

items.text: Sulphur, Z = 16: configuration 2, 8, 6; it gains 2 electrons to form S2- with configuration 2, 8, 8.
items.note: Gaining two completes the octet and gives the sulphide ion.

blocks.text: Electrovalent bonding occurs when an atom transfers one or more electrons to another, producing a positive ion and a negative ion that attract each other. Sodium chloride forms when sodium (2, 8, 1) gives its outer electron to chlorine (2, 8, 7): Na becomes Na+ (2, 8) and Cl becomes Cl- (2, 8, 8), and the opposite charges hold the ions in a giant crystal lattice. The bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between the ions. Because the ions are held in a lattice, electrovalent compounds have high melting points, conduct electricity when molten or dissolved (the ions become free to move), and many dissolve in water.

items: Electrovalency is the number of electrons lost or gained to reach a stable configuration.
Ionic compounds exist as lattices, not discrete molecules — the formula is the simplest ratio of ions.
Conductivity requires mobile ions: solid ionic compounds do not conduct, molten or aqueous ones do.
Electrovalent compounds are generally soluble in water and insoluble in organic solvents.
Electrostatic attraction between opposite charges is the electrovalent bond itself.

items.note: Each sodium atom transfers exactly one electron to one chlorine atom — the charges match 1:1.

items.text: Magnesium oxide: Mg (2, 8, 2) loses 2 electrons to O (2, 6), giving Mg2+ and O2-.
items.note: Two electrons transferred; the resulting charges are 2+ and 2-, so the ratio is 1:1 (MgO).

items.meaning: Number of electrons lost or gained by an atom to achieve a stable configuration.
Regular three-dimensional arrangement of ions in an ionic crystal.
Positively charged ion formed by loss of electrons.
Negatively charged ion formed by gain of electrons.

blocks.text: Covalent bonding occurs between non-metal atoms that both need electrons: neither can afford to transfer, so they share pairs of electrons instead. One shared pair is a single bond, two shared pairs a double bond and three a triple bond. In an orbit (dot-and-cross) structure each atom is drawn as a circle with its outer electrons, shared pairs are shown inside both circles, and each atom ends up with a count of eight (or two) including the shared pair. Hydrogen is the exception: with only the K shell it is satisfied by two electrons, one its own and one shared.

items: H2: one shared pair; each hydrogen reaches the stable duet of two.
O2: two shared pairs (double bond); each oxygen counts 8 including shared pairs.
N2: three shared pairs (triple bond); each nitrogen counts 8.
H2O: two single bonds, four shared pairs in total; the molecule is bent, not linear.
CH4: four single bonds; CO2: two double bonds; NH3: three single bonds plus one lone pair.
Covalent compounds are usually gases, liquids or low-melting solids; they do not conduct electricity because no ions are present.

items.text: Chlorine molecule Cl2: each chlorine contributes one electron to one shared pair, giving each an octet.
items.note: Each chlorine 'counts' the shared pair towards its own octet as well as its partner's — that is why sharing works.

items.text: Water H2O: oxygen shares one electron pair with each hydrogen; oxygen keeps two lone pairs.
items.note: Oxygen counts 8 (4 bonding electrons + 4 lone electrons); each hydrogen counts 2.

items.text: Nitrogen N2: three shared pairs form the triple bond, the strongest bond in this unit.
items.note: Breaking three shared pairs takes the most energy — hence nitrogen's chemical unreactivity.

items.meaning: A bond formed by sharing one or more pairs of electrons between two non-metal atoms.
A pair of electrons counted in the outer shell of both bonded atoms.
A pair of electrons in the outer shell that is not shared and belongs to one atom only.
A dot-and-cross diagram showing which electrons are shared and which are lone.

blocks.text: Properties follow from structure. Electrovalent compounds are giant lattices held by strong attraction between ions, so they need lots of energy to melt and conduct only when ions are free (molten or dissolved). Covalent compounds are discrete molecules held together inside by strong covalent bonds but between molecules only by weak forces, so they melt easily and, having no ions, never conduct. Solubility also differs: polar water dissolves ionic compounds well, while non-polar organic solvents dissolve many covalent substances. Selecting the bond type from the elements involved, then predicting the properties, is the standard exam chain of reasoning.

items: Metal + non-metal usually gives an electrovalent bond; non-metal + non-metal usually gives covalent.
High melting point and conductivity when molten/aqueous indicate ionic bonding.
Low melting point and no conductivity indicate simple molecular covalent bonding.
Diamond and graphite are covalent network solids — they are exceptions with very high melting points.
Ionic conductivity needs mobile ions; covalent substances never conduct because they have no charged particles free to move.

items.text: Sodium chloride melts at 801 degrees Celsius and conducts when molten; sugar melts at 186 degrees Celsius and never conducts.
items.note: The gap in melting point and the presence/absence of conduction both trace straight back to lattice ions versus discrete molecules.

items.text: Predicting from elements: calcium and chlorine are metal plus non-metal, so CaCl2 is electrovalent — high melting point, conducts when molten.
items.note: State the bond, then the structure, then the property — each step earns its own mark.

figures.caption: Figure: Electron transfer in sodium chloride
figures.description: Sodium (2, 8, 1) with one outer electron next to chlorine (2, 8, 7) with seven; the sodium electron transfers to chlorine, giving Na+ (2, 8) and Cl- (2, 8, 8), and the opposite charges attract.

figures.caption: Figure: Dot-and-cross structure of water
figures.description: Oxygen in the centre shares one electron pair with each hydrogen (two single bonds) and retains two lone pairs; oxygen counts eight electrons, each hydrogen two.

keyPoints: Z (protons) identifies the element; A (protons + neutrons) gives the mass number; neutrons = A - Z.
Isotopes have identical chemistry because their electron arrangements are identical.
The octet rule: atoms react to reach eight outer electrons (two for the K shell).
Electrovalent bonding is electron transfer between a metal and a non-metal, giving ions held in a lattice.
Ionic compounds conduct only when molten or dissolved, because only then are the ions mobile.
Covalent bonding is sharing of electron pairs between non-metal atoms.
One, two and three shared pairs give single, double and triple bonds.
Covalent compounds have no ions, so they do not conduct electricity.
Properties follow structure: lattice ions mean high melting points; discrete molecules mean low melting points.
examFocus: Configuration questions need the shell-by-shell working; do not write 2, 9 or any shell beyond capacity.
In orbit-structure answers, count the shared pair for both atoms and show lone pairs — diagrams without lone pairs lose marks.
Property questions must chain reasoning: bond type -> structure -> property, not just state the property.
Isotope calculations: neutrons = A - Z, and average atomic mass uses percentage abundance of each isotope.

vocabulary.meaning: Same element, same Z, different neutron count.
Eight electrons in the outer shell — the stable arrangement.
Electrons lost or gained to reach stability.
Shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms.
Unshared electron pair belonging to one atom.
Dot-and-cross diagram of a molecule's bonding.

questions.prompt: An atom of an element has atomic number 12 and mass number 24. The number of neutrons is:
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 24 - 12 = 12. This is magnesium-24.
questions.commonMistake: Reading mass number as the neutron count; neutrons exclude the protons.

questions.prompt: Which electronic configuration belongs to an ion of an element in group 1?
questions.explanation: Group 1 elements have one outer electron; losing it gives a cation with a full outer shell such as 2, 8, 8 (for potassium) or 2, 8 (for sodium).
questions.commonMistake: Choosing 2, 8, 1 — that is the neutral atom, not the ion.

options: Only when molten or in solution
questions.answer: Only when molten or in solution
questions.explanation: Conduction needs mobile ions; in the solid lattice the ions are fixed in place, but melting or dissolving frees them to carry charge.
questions.commonMistake: Saying 'never' because it is a non-metal plus metal — conductivity depends on ion mobility, not on the elements.

questions.prompt: How many shared electron pairs are present in a molecule of nitrogen, N2?
questions.explanation: Each nitrogen has 5 outer electrons and needs 8, so the atoms share three pairs — a triple bond.
questions.commonMistake: Counting only one pair because there is one bond drawn; three pairs are shared to complete both octets.

questions.prompt: Isotopes of the same element have:
questions.explanation: Isotopes differ only in neutron count; identical proton number means identical electronic configuration, and configuration governs chemistry.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing different chemical properties because the nuclei differ — nuclear differences affect radioactivity, not chemistry.

questions.prompt: Which compound is held together by electrovalent bonds?
questions.explanation: Magnesium is a metal and oxygen a non-metal; magnesium transfers two electrons to oxygen, forming Mg2+ and O2- ions.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming every compound with two elements is ionic — the metal/non-metal split decides.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: chlorine has atomic number 17, so its electronic configuration is ________, ________ and ________.
questions.explanation: Seventeen electrons fill K with 2, L with 8 and leave 7 in M; seven outer electrons mean chlorine needs one more to complete its octet.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 2, 8, 8 — that is the chloride ion after gaining an electron, not the neutral atom.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the covalent molecule HCl, ________ electrons are shared between the two atoms, and chlorine additionally holds ________ lone pair(s).
questions.explanation: Hydrogen shares one electron with chlorine to reach its duet; chlorine contributes one electron to the shared pair and keeps its three remaining pairs as lone pairs.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting the lone pairs — the shared pair completes hydrogen's duet while chlorine's octet needs its own three lone pairs counted as well.

questions.prompt: Define atomic number and mass number, and find the number of neutrons in an atom with Z = 19 and A = 39.
questions.answer: Atomic number (Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus, which identifies the element. Mass number (A) is the total number of protons and neutrons. Neutrons = A - Z = 39 - 19 = 20.
questions.explanation: The two counts together locate every particle: protons from Z, neutrons by subtraction, and electrons equal to protons in a neutral atom.
questions.commonMistake: Quoting definitions without connecting them to the calculation — both definition and subtraction are needed.

questions.prompt: Explain, in terms of electrons, how a sodium atom becomes Na+ and a chlorine atom becomes Cl-, and state the force that holds the two ions together.
questions.answer: Sodium (2, 8, 1) has one electron more than a stable octet; it loses that electron to become Na+ with configuration 2, 8 and a 1+ charge. Chlorine (2, 8, 7) needs one electron to complete its octet; it gains the electron given up by sodium to become Cl- with configuration 2, 8, 8 and a 1- charge. The electrovalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions.
questions.explanation: Both changes are driven by the octet rule: one atom loses, the other gains, and the resulting opposite charges attract.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the attraction as 'the transferred electron' — the electron is no longer shared; the attraction is between the ions.

questions.prompt: Draw or describe the orbit structure of carbon dioxide, CO2, stating the number of double bonds and how each atom achieves an octet.
questions.answer: Carbon is in the centre, double-bonded to each oxygen: O=C=O. Each double bond is two shared pairs, so carbon shares four pairs in total and counts 8 electrons; each oxygen shares two pairs with carbon and keeps two lone pairs, also counting 8.
questions.explanation: Carbon has 4 outer electrons and needs 4 more, satisfied by two double bonds; each oxygen has 6 and needs 2, satisfied by one double bond plus its lone pairs.
questions.commonMistake: Drawing single bonds from carbon to each oxygen, which leaves carbon with only six electrons.

questions.prompt: Compare the melting point and electrical conductivity of sodium chloride and methane, and explain both differences.
questions.answer: Sodium chloride has a very high melting point because it is a giant lattice of Na+ and Cl- ions with strong electrostatic attraction throughout; it conducts when molten or dissolved because the ions are then free to move. Methane has a low melting point because it consists of discrete CH4 molecules held only by weak forces between molecules; it never conducts because it contains no ions or free electrons.
questions.explanation: Structure determines properties: ionic lattices need large energy to break, and conduction requires mobile charged particles.
questions.commonMistake: Stating the differences without the structural explanation, which is where most marks are allocated.

questions.prompt: Explain why an atom of calcium (Z = 20) forms a Ca2+ ion rather than Ca+, why a chlorine atom forms Cl- rather than Cl+, and describe the bonding in calcium chloride.
questions.answer: Calcium has configuration 2, 8, 8, 2. It loses both outer electrons to reach the stable noble-gas configuration of argon (2, 8, 8); a singly ionised Ca+ would still have an outer shell that is neither empty nor full, whereas Ca2+ completes the octet, and the energy released when the Ca2+ ion attracts two Cl- ions in the lattice makes the second electron loss worthwhile. Chlorine (2, 8, 7) gains one electron to reach the octet 2, 8, 8, forming Cl-; forming Cl+ would mean giving up an electron and moving further from the octet, so it does not occur. In calcium chloride each calcium transfers one electron to each of two chlorine atoms, giving Ca2+ and two Cl- ions held in an electrovalent lattice with the formula CaCl2.
questions.explanation: Every step is judged against the octet rule: ions form only when the result is a full outer shell, and the formula follows from charge balance.
questions.commonMistake: Saying calcium forms Ca2+ 'because it is in group 2' without stating the electron-configuration reason.

questions.prompt: Why do covalent compounds generally have low melting points even though the covalent bonds within their molecules are strong?
questions.answer: Melting a covalent compound does not break the covalent bonds inside the molecules; it only overcomes the weak forces between one molecule and its neighbours. Because those intermolecular forces are weak, little energy is needed and melting points are low. The strong covalent bonds are broken only in chemical reactions such as burning, not by melting.
questions.explanation: The distinction between intramolecular bonds (strong, within molecules) and intermolecular forces (weak, between molecules) explains the paradox.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming melting breaks every bond — identifying which bonds melting actually affects is the core of the answer.
